newsitem.title: USA: Senators propose public financing of campaigns.
newsitem.headline: Senators propose public financing of campaigns.

text.p: A group of Democratic senators proposed Tuesday to finance political campaigns with public money as a way to fix what they called a broken system.

But the group acknowledged the proposed legislation will have a tough road ahead, since there is not momentum yet for campaign finance reform despite the growing scandal over questionable and illegal donations to President Clinton's Democratic Party for last year's campaign.
Sen. John Kerry, a Massachusetts Democrat, said "the system is broken ... our democracy is in trouble" and the way campaigns are financed needs a total overhaul.
He said there should be "a total break" from having business and other special interests give huge amounts of private money to finance campaigns, which he and the others claim corrupt the system.

Kerry was joined by Ohio Democratic Sen. John Glenn, Minnesota Democratic Sen. Paul Wellstone, Arkansas Democratic Sen. Dale Bumpers and Rhode Island Democratic Sen. Jack Reed to offer what they called a "clean money ... clean elections" plan they will introduce in the Senate.
The plan is based on a plan adopted in Maine to get candidates to get signatures on petitions and token $5 contributions from thousands of constituents to qualify for public funds.

Wellstone estimated at a news conference attended by some major civic and church organizations that the plan would cost about $160 million to finance Senate campaigns. Their legislation applies only to the Senate and they said separate legislation applying to the House would be introduced.
This group of Democrats also supports another campaign financing plan sponsored in the Senate by Republican John McCain of Arizona and Democrat Russ Feingold of Wisconsin.

Clinton supports the McCain-Feingold plan and Monday appointed former Democratic Vice President Walter Mondale and former Kansas Republican Sen. Nancy Kassebaum Baker to head a drive to drum up support for passage of campaign reforms by July 4.
